claim: Heterotrimeric G proteins are molecular switches that play pivotal roles in signaling processes from vision to olfaction and neurotransmission.
source: Heterotrimeric G proteins are molecular switches that play pivotal roles in signaling processes from vision to olfaction and neurotransmission (Oldham and Hamm, 2006; Oldham and Hamm, 2008; Johnston and Siderovski, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Oldham and Hamm, 2006; Oldham and Hamm, 2008; Johnston and Siderovski, 2007).

claim: By default, a G protein adopts an inactive state in which guanosine diphosphate (GDP) binds between the Ras-like and helical domains of the α-subunit (Gα).
source: By default, a G protein adopts an inactive state in which guanosine diphosphate (GDP) binds between the Ras-like and helical domains of the α-subunit (Gα, Figure 1).
evidence: The claim references Figure 1 which shows the structural organization of Gα with GDP binding site, and is based on established structural knowledge.

claim: A dimer consisting of the β- and γ-subunits (Gβγ) also binds Gα.
source: A dimer consisting of the β- and γ-subunits (Gβγ) also binds Gα.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the structure of heterotrimeric G proteins.

claim: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) trigger G-protein activation by binding Gα and stimulating GDP release, followed by GTP binding to Gα and dissociation of Gα from Gβγ.
source: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) trigger G-protein activation by binding Gα and stimulating GDP release, followed by GTP binding to Gα and dissociation of Gα from Gβγ.
evidence: This describes the established mechanism of G protein activation, which is well-known in the field.

claim: Gα and Gβγ interact with effectors that trigger downstream cellular responses.
source: Gα and Gβγ then interact with effectors that trigger downstream cellular responses.
evidence: This is established knowledge about G protein signaling.

claim: Gα returns to the inactive state by hydrolyzing GTP to GDP and rebinding Gβγ.
source: Gα returns to the inactive state by hydrolyzing GTP to GDP and rebinding Gβγ.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the G protein cycle.

claim: A common Gα numbering scheme (CGN) has been established to facilitate discussion of the activation mechanisms of different Gα homologs.
source: Given the central role Gα plays, a common Gα numbering scheme (CGN) has been established to facilitate discussion of the activation mechanisms of different Gα homologs (Flock et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Flock et al., 2015.

claim: The GPCR- and nucleotide-binding sites of Gα are ~30 Å apart.
source: Strikingly, the GPCR- and nucleotide-binding sites of Gα are ~30 Å apart (Figure 1), but the allosteric mechanism coupling these sites to evoke GDP release remains incompletely understood (Oldham and Hamm, 2008).
evidence: The claim references Figure 1 and is supported by citation to Oldham and Hamm, 2008.

claim: The allosteric mechanism coupling the GPCR- and nucleotide-binding sites to evoke GDP release remains incompletely understood.
source: Strikingly, the GPCR- and nucleotide-binding sites of Gα are ~30 Å apart (Figure 1), but the allosteric mechanism coupling these sites to evoke GDP release remains incompletely understood (Oldham and Hamm, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Oldham and Hamm, 2008.

claim: Early studies of Gα subunits revealed structures of the GDP- and GTP-bound states, as well as the transition state for GTP hydrolysis.
source: Early studies of Gα subunits revealed structures of the GDP- and GTP-bound states, as well as the transition state for GTP hydrolysis (Sunahara et al., 1997; Leipe et al., 2002; Westfield et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Sunahara et al., 1997; Leipe et al., 2002; Westfield et al., 2011).

claim: The high similarity of GDP- and GTP-bound structures and the binding of GDP or GTP deep in the protein's core suggests that activation occurs by adoption of other conformational states that allow GDP release.
source: The high similarity of these structures and the binding of GDP or GTP deep in the protein's core suggests that activation occurs by adoption of other conformational states that allow GDP release (Lambright et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lambright et al., 1994 and represents an inference from structural data.

claim: The first crystal structure of a GPCR-bound G protein showed the Ras-like and helical domains of Gα hinged apart and GDP dissociated.
source: One intermediate in G protein activation was suggested by the first crystal structure of a GPCR-bound G protein in which the Ras-like and helical domains of Gα are hinged apart and GDP has dissociated (Rasmussen et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rasmussen et al., 2011.

claim: A universal mechanism for G protein activation has been proposed in which GPCR binding induces translation of H5 away from H1, which increases disorder in H1 and the P-loop to facilitate GDP release.
source: Structural analysis has led to the proposal of a universal mechanism for G protein activation (Flock et al., 2015). In this model, GPCR binding induces translation of H5 away from H1, which increases disorder in H1 and the P-loop (or Walker A motif [Leipe et al., 2002]) to facilitate GDP release.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Flock et al., 2015 and Leipe et al., 2002.

claim: There is evidence that additional intermediates may be involved in Gα activation.
source: However, there is evidence that additional intermediates may be involved in Gα activation, (Oldham and Hamm, 2008; Westfield et al., 2011; Liang et al., 2017; Hilger et al., 2018) and the functional importance of this conformational ensemble has been previously suggested (Furness et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Oldham and Hamm, 2008; Westfield et al., 2011; Liang et al., 2017; Hilger et al., 2018).

claim: The functional importance of a conformational ensemble in G protein activation has been previously suggested.
source: However, there is evidence that additional intermediates may be involved in Gα activation, (Oldham and Hamm, 2008; Westfield et al., 2011; Liang et al., 2017; Hilger et al., 2018) and the functional importance of this conformational ensemble has been previously suggested (Furness et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Furness et al., 2016.

claim: Mutagenesis and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) studies have suggested important roles for structural elements other than H5 and the P-loop.
source: Furthermore, mutagenesis and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) studies have suggested important roles for other structural elements (Toyama et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2015; Goricanec et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Toyama et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2015; Goricanec et al., 2016).

claim: Methodological advances now enable simulations to capture millisecond timescale processes for proteins with less than 100 residues.
source: Methodological advances now enable simulations to capture millisecond timescale processes for proteins with less than 100 residues (Lindorff-Larsen et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lindorff-Larsen et al., 2011.

claim: It is now possible to capture the binding or release of small molecules from small proteins using molecular dynamics simulations.
source: For example, it is now possible to capture the binding or release of small molecules (Buch et al., 2011; Bowman and Geissler, 2012; Silva et al., 2011; Plattner and Noé, 2015; Tiwary et al., 2015) and peptides (Plattner et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2017) from small proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Buch et al., 2011; Bowman and Geissler, 2012; Silva et al., 2011; Plattner and Noé, 2015; Tiwary et al., 2015).

claim: Simulations on the ANTON supercomputer have revealed critical conformational dynamics of G proteins in their inactive and active states, elucidating the role of domain opening in GDP unbinding.
source: Impressive simulations on the ANTON supercomputer have revealed critical conformational dynamics of G proteins in their inactive and active states, elucidating the role of domain opening in GDP unbinding (Dror et al., 2015; Yao et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dror et al., 2015 and Yao et al., 2016.

claim: Even the ANTON supercomputer could not capture the entire process of G protein activation and GDP release due to the size of the Gα subunit (>300 residues) and the slow kinetics of GDP dissociation (~10−3 min−1).
source: However, even this specialized hardware could not capture the entire process of G protein activation and GDP release due to the size of the Gα subunit (>300 residues) and the slow kinetics of GDP dissociation (~10−3 min−1) (Chidiac et al., 1999; Ross, 2008; Mukhopadhyay and Ross, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies reporting GDP dissociation kinetics (Chidiac et al., 1999; Ross, 2008; Mukhopadhyay and Ross, 1999).

claim: Gαq has one of the slowest GDP release rates.
source: As a test of this methodology, we apply it to Gαq, which has one of the slowest GDP release rates (Chidiac et al., 1999) and is frequently mutated in uveal melanoma (Van Raamsdonk et al., 2009; Van Raamsdonk et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chidiac et al., 1999.

claim: Gαq is frequently mutated in uveal melanoma.
source: As a test of this methodology, we apply it to Gαq, which has one of the slowest GDP release rates (Chidiac et al., 1999) and is frequently mutated in uveal melanoma (Van Raamsdonk et al., 2009; Van Raamsdonk et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Van Raamsdonk et al., 2009 and Van Raamsdonk et al., 2010.

claim: The authors combined metadynamics, Markov state models (MSMs), and CARDS analysis to construct an atomically detailed model of G protein activation.
source: We construct an atomically detailed model of G protein activation by combining three powerful computational methods: metadynamics, Markov state models (MSMs), and CARDS analysis of correlated motions.
evidence: The claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: The rate-limiting step for GDP release correlates with tilting rather than translation of the GPCR-binding helix 5.
source: Surprisingly, the rate-limiting step for GDP release correlates with tilting rather than translation of the GPCR-binding helix 5.
evidence: This is a key finding from the study's simulations and analysis.

claim: β-Strands 1 – 3 and helix 1 emerge as hubs in the allosteric network that links conformational changes in the GPCR-binding site to disordering of the distal nucleotide-binding site and consequent GDP release.
source: β-Strands 1 – 3 and helix 1 emerge as hubs in the allosteric network that links conformational changes in the GPCR-binding site to disordering of the distal nucleotide-binding site and consequent GDP release.
evidence: This is a key finding from the study's CARDS analysis.

claim: Studying the mechanism of spontaneous GDP release from a truncated form of Gαq would be representative of the mechanism of GPCR-mediated activation of the heterotrimeric G protein.
source: We reasoned that studying the mechanism of spontaneous GDP release from a truncated form of Gαq would be representative of the mechanism of GPCR-mediated activation of the heterotrimeric G protein while minimizing the computational cost of our simulations.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on previous work and reasoning about protein dynamics.

claim: A protein's spontaneous fluctuations are representative of the conformational changes required for the protein to perform its function.
source: This hypothesis was inspired by previous work demonstrating that a protein's spontaneous fluctuations are representative of the conformational changes required for the protein to perform its function (Boehr et al., 2006; Fraser et al., 2009; Changeux and Edelstein, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Boehr et al., 2006; Fraser et al., 2009; Changeux and Edelstein, 2011).

claim: GPCRs stabilize conformational states that G proteins naturally, albeit infrequently, adopt in the absence of a receptor.
source: Therefore, we hypothesized that GPCRs stabilize conformational states that G proteins naturally, albeit infrequently, adopt in the absence of a receptor.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the principle of conformational selection.

claim: Gα forms substantial interactions with GPCRs, compared to the relatively negligible interactions between GPCRs and G protein β and γ subunits.
source: We chose to focus on Gα since it forms substantial interactions with GPCRs, compared to the relatively negligible interactions between GPCRs and G protein β and γ subunits.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of GPCR-G protein interactions.

claim: GPCRs and 'mini' G proteins, essentially composed of just the Ras-like domain of Gα, recapitulate many features of GPCR-G protein interactions.
source: This view is supported by the fact that GPCRs and 'mini' G proteins, essentially composed of just the Ras-like domain of Gα, recapitulate many features of GPCR-G protein interactions (Carpenter et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Carpenter et al., 2016.

claim: The last five residues of Gαq contact Gα in some GDP-bound structures but not in GPCR-bound structures.
source: These residues contact Gα in some GDP-bound structures but not in GPCR-bound structures, (Lambright et al., 1996; Noel et al., 1993) and removing these residues promotes GDP release due to a reduced GDP-binding affinity (Denker et al., 1992; Marin et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to structural studies (Lambright et al., 1996; Noel et al., 1993).

claim: Removing the last five residues of Gαq promotes GDP release due to a reduced GDP-binding affinity.
source: These residues contact Gα in some GDP-bound structures but not in GPCR-bound structures, (Lambright et al., 1996; Noel et al., 1993) and removing these residues promotes GDP release due to a reduced GDP-binding affinity (Denker et al., 1992; Marin et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Denker et al., 1992 and Marin et al., 2002.

claim: The last five residues of Gαq help stabilize the inactive state.
source: Taken together, such evidence suggests that the last five residues of Gαq help stabilize the inactive state and that removing them would accelerate activation.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural and biochemical data cited in the manuscript.

claim: The energetic barrier to GDP release is lower in metadynamics simulations of the truncated variant than for full-length Gαq.
source: In support of this hypothesis, we find that the energetic barrier to GDP release is lower in metadynamics simulations of the truncated variant than for full-length Gαq (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Metadynamics facilitates broad sampling of conformational space by biasing simulations to sample conformations with different distances between GDP and Gαq.
source: First, we use metadynamics (Tiwary et al., 2015; Laio and Parrinello, 2002; Dama et al., 2014) to facilitate broad sampling of conformational space by biasing simulations to sample conformations with different distances between GDP and Gαq.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study, with citations to relevant literature.

claim: Adding a biasing force in metadynamics can distort the system's kinetics or cause the simulations to sample high-energy conformations that are not representative of behavior at thermal equilibrium.
source: Doing so forces GDP release to occur but provides limited mechanistic information because adding a biasing force can distort the system's kinetics or cause the simulations to sample high-energy conformations that are not representative of behavior at thermal equilibrium.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the limitations of metadynamics.

claim: The authors used conformations along release pathways observed by metadynamics as starting points for standard molecular dynamics simulations, yielding an aggregate simulation time of 122.6 μs.
source: To overcome these limitations, we chose starting conformations along release pathways observed by metadynamics as starting points for standard molecular dynamics simulations, together yielding an aggregate simulation time of 122.6 μs.
evidence: This describes the methodology and simulation time achieved in the study.

claim: MSMs are adept at extracting both thermodynamic and kinetic information from many standard simulations that, together, cover larger regions of conformational space than any individual simulation.
source: Then we use these simulations to build an MSM (Source data 1). MSMs are adept at extracting both thermodynamic and kinetic information from many standard simulations that, together, cover larger regions of conformational space than any individual simulation (Bowman et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bowman et al., 2014.

claim: Related approaches to combining metadynamics and MSMs have successfully captured the dynamics of small model systems and RNA polymerase.
source: Related approaches have successfully captured the dynamics of small model systems (Biswas et al., 2018) and RNA polymerase (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Biswas et al., 2018 and Zhang et al., 2016.

claim: The authors captured the entire mechanism of G-protein activation, including GDP release and the rate-limiting step for this process.
source: This protocol enabled us to capture the entire mechanism of G-protein activation, including GDP release and the rate-limiting step for this process.
evidence: This is a key result of the study's computational approach.

claim: GDP release is the rate-limiting step for G-protein activation and downstream signaling.
source: Identifying the rate-limiting step for this process is of great value because GDP release is the rate-limiting step for G-protein activation and downstream signaling.
evidence: This is established knowledge about G protein activation.

claim: The bound state is defined as all conformations where the distance from the center of mass of GDP's phosphates to the center of mass of three residues on H1 (Lys52G.H1.1, Ser53G.H1.2, and Thr54G.H1.3) is less than 8 Å.
source: By comparing the structures before and after the rate-limiting step, we define the bound state as all conformations where the distance from the center of mass of GDP's phosphates to the center of mass of three residues on H1 that contact the GDP β-phosphate (Lys52G.H1.1, Ser53G.H1.2, and Thr54G.H1.3) is less than 8 Å.
evidence: This describes the operational definition used in the study's analysis.

claim: The distance from GDP's phosphates to H1 residues remains less than 8 Å throughout 35.3 μs of GDP-bound simulations.
source: Consistent with this definition, this distance remains less than 8 Å throughout the entirety of 35.3 μs of GDP-bound simulations.
evidence: This is data from the simulations supporting the definition of the bound state.

claim: The Ras-like and helical domains separate during the rate-limiting step for GDP release.
source: For example, we observe that the Ras-like and helical domains separate (Figure 2C and Source data 3), as observed in DEER experiments (Van Eps et al., 2011) and previous simulations (Dror et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and Source data 3, and is consistent with previous experimental and computational studies.

claim: Domain separation is driven by the disruption of multiple inter-domain interactions.
source: This finding is consistent with the intuition that these domains must separate to sterically permit GDP release, and that this separation is driven by the disruption of multiple inter-domain interactions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed structural changes.

claim: A salt bridge between K275G.s5hg.1 and D155H.hdhe.5 is disrupted during domain opening.
source: For example, we note a disrupted salt bridge between K275G.s5hg.1 and D155H.hdhe.5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), previously identified in structural studies (Flock et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4 and a citation to Flock et al., 2015.

claim: Domain opening is accompanied by disruption of a key salt bridge between Glu49G.s1h1.4 of the P-loop and Arg183G.hfs2.2 of switch 1.
source: Domain opening is accompanied by disruption of a key salt bridge between Glu49G.s1h1.4 of the P-loop and Arg183G.hfs2.2 of switch 1 (Figure 2D and Source data 3), as well as an increase in the disorder of many of the surrounding residues (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), consistent with the proposal that this salt bridge stabilizes the closed, GDP-bound state (Liang et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D, Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A, and Source data 3, and is consistent with a previous study (Liang et al., 2017).

claim: The salt bridge between Glu49G.s1h1.4 and Arg183G.hfs2.2 stabilizes the closed, GDP-bound state.
source: Domain opening is accompanied by disruption of a key salt bridge between Glu49G.s1h1.4 of the P-loop and Arg183G.hfs2.2 of switch 1 (Figure 2D and Source data 3), as well as an increase in the disorder of many of the surrounding residues (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), consistent with the proposal that this salt bridge stabilizes the closed, GDP-bound state (Liang et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Liang et al., 2017.

claim: Domain opening is necessary but not sufficient for GDP unbinding.
source: While domain opening is necessary for GDP release, previous simulations suggest it is insufficient for unbinding (Dror et al., 2015). Indeed, we also see that this opening is necessary but not sufficient for GDP unbinding, as the Ras-like and helical domains often separate prior to release (Figure 2C and Source data 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and Source data 3, and is consistent with previous simulations (Dror et al., 2015).

claim: The Ras-like and helical domains only separate by ~10 Å during the rate-limiting step.
source: Notably, the Ras-like and helical domains only separate by ~10 Å during the rate-limiting step.
evidence: This is data from the simulations.

claim: GDP release may have occurred long before a G protein adopts the widely opened conformations observed in crystallographic structures.
source: This result suggests that GDP release may have occurred long before a G protein adopts the sort of widely opened conformations observed in crystallographic structures (Rasmussen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of domain separation distances in simulations versus crystal structures.

claim: H5 tilts by about 26° during the rate-limiting step for GDP release.
source: The most striking is tilting of H5 by about 26° (Figure 3A, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: H5 tilting correlates strongly with the distance between GDP and Gαq along the highest flux dissociation pathway.
source: We find that H5 tilting correlates strongly with the distance between GDP and Gαq along the highest flux dissociation pathway (Figure 3B and Source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and Source data 1.

claim: Substantial tilting of H5 is coincident with the rate-limiting step for GDP release.
source: In particular, substantial tilting of H5 is coincident with the rate-limiting step for GDP release.
evidence: This is a key finding from the study's analysis of the simulations.

claim: In X-ray structures and the universal mechanism, H5 is proposed to translate along its helical axis towards the GPCR, initiating the process of GDP release.
source: This tilting contrasts with X-ray structures and the universal mechanism, in which H5 is proposed to translate along its helical axis towards the GPCR, initiating the process of GDP release (Figure 3A).
evidence: This describes the previously proposed mechanism, with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: Translation of H5 is not correlated with the rate-limiting step of GDP release.
source: During our simulations we also observe translation of H5, but it is not correlated with the rate-limiting step of GDP release (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, and Source data 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, and Source data 3.

claim: A crystal structure of rhodopsin with a C-terminal fragment from H5 of Gαt shows a similar degree of tilting to that observed in the simulations.
source: For example, a crystal structure of rhodopsin (Choe et al., 2011) with a C-terminal fragment from H5 of Gαt shows a similar degree of tilting (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Choe et al., 2011 and reference to Figure 3A.

claim: The tilt of H5 varies in crystal structures of the β2AR-Gs complex, two different GLP-1 receptor-Gs complexes, and an A2AR-mini-Gs complex.
source: Also, the tilt of H5 varies in crystal structures of the β2AR-Gs complex (Rasmussen et al., 2011), two different GLP-1 receptor-Gs complexes (Liang et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2017), and an A2AR-mini-Gs complex (Carpenter et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple crystal structures (Rasmussen et al., 2011; Liang et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2017; Carpenter et al., 2016).

claim: The potential relevance of H5 tilting has been acknowledged by a number of recent works.
source: The potential relevance of tilting has also been acknowledged by a number of recent works (Flock et al., 2015; Rasmussen et al., 2011; Oldham et al., 2006) including four recently published structures of receptor-G-protein complexes across which H5 also shows a broad range of tilting and translational motion (Koehl et al., 2018; Draper-Joyce et al., 2018; García-Nafría et al., 2018; Kang et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Flock et al., 2015; Rasmussen et al., 2011; Oldham et al., 2006; Koehl et al., 2018; Draper-Joyce et al., 2018; García-Nafría et al., 2018; Kang et al., 2018).

claim: The tilting and translation observed in the simulations falls within the observed range of tilting and translational motions that H5 undergoes in available GPCR-G protein complex structures.
source: Interestingly, the tilting and translation we observe falls within the observed range of tilting and translational motions that H5 undergoes in available GPCR-G protein complex structures (Rasmussen et al., 2011; Koehl et al., 2018; Draper-Joyce et al., 2018; García-Nafría et al., 2018; Kang et al., 2018), providing support that conformational selection plays an important role (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with crystal structures (Rasmussen et al., 2011; Koehl et al., 2018; Draper-Joyce et al., 2018; García-Nafría et al., 2018; Kang et al., 2018) and data shown in Figure 3—source data 1.

claim: In the A2AR-mini-Gs structure, H5 is translated toward the GPCR but GDP remains bound.
source: Finally, H5 is translated toward the GPCR in the A2AR-mini-Gs structure but GDP remains bound (Carpenter et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Carpenter et al., 2016.

claim: Amino acid substitutions required to create mini-Gs may mitigate H5 tilting.
source: However, given that we see GDP release without H5 translation in our simulations, it is also possible that amino acid substitutions required to create mini-Gs instead mitigate H5 tilting.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the simulation results and the observation that mini-Gs shows H5 translation without GDP release.

claim: Some of the mutations in mini-Gs stabilize the GDP-bound state.
source: Both of these models are consistent with the fact that some of the mutations in mini-Gs stabilize the GDP-bound state (Sun et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sun et al., 2015.

claim: Tilting of H5 is an early step in the GDP release process, which is followed by upward translation of this helix to form a GPCR-G protein complex primed to bind GTP.
source: We propose that tilting of H5 is an early step in the GDP release process, which is followed by upward translation of this helix to form a GPCR-G protein complex primed to bind GTP.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the simulation results.

claim: Tilting of H5 is coincident with the rate-limiting step for GDP release, while translation of H5 only becomes stable after GDP dissociates.
source: This hypothesis stems from our observation that tilting of H5 is coincident with the rate-limiting step for GDP release, while translation of H5 only becomes stable after GDP dissociates (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: G-protein activation occurs through a series of sequential interactions with a GPCR.
source: This model is consistent with previous suggestions that G-protein activation occurs through a series of sequential interactions with a GPCR (Oldham and Hamm, 2008; Rasmussen et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Oldham and Hamm, 2008 and Rasmussen et al., 2011.

claim: Any displacement of H5, whether tilting or translation, may be sufficient to trigger GDP release.
source: Another possibility is that any displacement of H5, whether tilting or translation, may be sufficient to trigger GDP release.
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: The hypothesis that spontaneous motions of a protein encode functionally relevant conformational changes suggests that the coupling between the GPCR- and nucleotide-binding sites of Gα should be present in simulations of the inactive protein.
source: Our hypothesis that spontaneous motions of a protein encode functionally relevant conformational changes suggests that the coupling between the GPCR- and nucleotide-binding sites of Gα should be present in simulations of the inactive protein; This provides a means to identify key elements of this allosteric network.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the principle of conformational dynamics.

claim: The authors ran 35.3 µs of simulation of GDP-Gαq to identify the allosteric network.
source: To test this hypothesis, we ran 35.3 µs of simulation of GDP-Gαq.
evidence: This describes the simulation time used for the CARDS analysis.

claim: CARDS detects correlations between both the structure and dynamical states of every pair of dihedral angles.
source: Then we applied the CARDS method (Singh and Bowman, 2017) to detect correlations between both the structure and dynamical states of every pair of dihedral angles.
evidence: This describes the CARDS methodology, with a citation to Singh and Bowman, 2017.

claim: Tilting of H5 directly communicates with and impacts the conformational preferences of the s6h5 loop, which contacts the nucleobase of GDP.
source: This analysis reveals that tilting of H5 directly communicates with and impacts the conformational preferences of the s6h5 loop, which contacts the nucleobase of GDP (Figure 4, Figure 5, Source data 2, and Source data 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4, Figure 5, Source data 2, and Source data 3.

claim: During the rate-limiting step, contacts between the s6h5 loop and GDP are broken and there is increased disorder in the s6h5 loop, particularly Ala331 of the TCAT motif.
source: During the rate-limiting step, these contacts are broken and there is increased disorder in the s6h5 loop, particularly Ala331 of the TCAT motif (Figure 5 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Mutating the TCAT motif accelerates GDP release.
source: The importance of the TCAT motif in our model is consistent with its conservation and the fact that mutating it accelerates GDP release (Iiri et al., 1994; Posner et al., 1998; Thomas et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Iiri et al., 1994; Posner et al., 1998; Thomas et al., 1993.

claim: Mutations in the TCAT motif accelerate GDP release by weakening shape complementarity with GDP.
source: Based on our model, we propose these mutations accelerate release by weakening shape complementarity with GDP.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the simulation results.

claim: H1 is strongly coupled with the s6h5 loop.
source: We also observe an important role for communication from H5 to H1, consistent with the universal mechanism. In particular, H1 is strongly coupled with the s6h5 loop (Figure 4B and Source data 2), which is sensitive to displacement of H5.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B and Source data 2.

claim: In the rate-limiting step, s6h5 moves away from H1, contributing to an increase in disorder of H1 and the P-loop.
source: In the rate-limiting step, s6h5 moves away from H1, contributing to an increase in disorder of H1 and the P-loop (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Increased disorder in residues that directly contact the GDP phosphates (Glu49G.s1h1.4, Ser50G.s1h1.5, Gly51G.s1h1.6, Lys52G.H1.1, and Ser53G.H1.2) likely contributes to a reduced affinity for GDP.
source: Increased disorder in a set of residues that directly contact the GDP phosphates (Glu49G.s1h1.4, Ser50G.s1h1.5, Gly51G.s1h1.6, Lys52G.H1.1, and Ser53G.H1.2) likely contributes to a reduced affinity for GDP (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).

claim: Increased disorder in H1 and P-loop residues contributes to disruption of the salt bridge between Glu49G.s1h1.4 of the Ras-like domain and Arg183G.hfs2.2 of the helical domain, facilitating inter-domain separation.
source: Increased disorder in these residues also contributes to disruption of the salt bridge between Glu49G.s1h1.4 of the Ras-like domain and Arg183G.hfs2.2 of the helical domain, facilitating inter-domain separation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed structural and dynamical changes.

claim: The s6h5 loop impacts the nucleotide-binding site through allosteric coupling with the HG helix, which also contacts GDP via Lys275G.s5hg.1 and Asp277G.HG.2.
source: We further note that the s6h5 loop impacts the nucleotide-binding site through allosteric coupling with the HG helix, which also contacts GDP via Lys275G.s5hg.1 and Asp277G.HG.2 (Figures 4E and 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 4E and 6.

claim: The disorder of Lys275G.s5hg.1 and Asp277G.HG.2 increases during the rate-limiting step.
source: The disorder of both of these residues increases during the rate-limiting step, consistent with observations of increased mobility in HG upon receptor-mediated activation (Oldham and Hamm, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data and is consistent with previous observations (Oldham and Hamm, 2008).

claim: There are correlations between the P-loop and Lys275G.s5hg.1 on Helix G.
source: There are also correlations between the P-loop and Lys275G.s5hg.1 on Helix G (Figure 4E and Source data 2), which result from the disruption of a key salt bridge between Lys275G.s5hg.1 and Glu49G.s1h1.4 on the P-loop during the rate-limiting step (Figure 6 and Source data 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E, Figure 6, Source data 2, and Source data 3.

claim: A salt bridge between Lys275G.s5hg.1 and Glu49G.s1h1.4 is disrupted during the rate-limiting step.
source: There are also correlations between the P-loop and Lys275G.s5hg.1 on Helix G (Figure 4E and Source data 2), which result from the disruption of a key salt bridge between Lys275G.s5hg.1 and Glu49G.s1h1.4 on the P-loop during the rate-limiting step (Figure 6 and Source data 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6 and Source data 3.

claim: Lys275G.s5hg.1 is conserved across all Gα families.
source: Lys275G.s5hg.1 is conserved across all Gα families, suggesting it plays an important role in the stability or function of the protein.

claim: Attempts to experimentally examine the role of Lys275G.s5hg.1 by mutation have resulted in aggregation.
source: However, attempts to experimentally examine the role of this residue by mutating Lys275G.s5hg.1 have resulted in aggregation (Sun et al., 2015).

claim: Lys275G.s5hg.1 plays an important role in stabilizing the GDP-bound state and breaking the salt bridge with Glu49G.s1h1.4 facilitates GDP release.
source: Our simulations suggest Lys275G.s5hg.1 plays an important role in stabilizing the GDP-bound state and that breaking the salt bridge with Glu49G.s1h1.4 facilitates GDP release.
evidence: This is an inference based on the simulation results.

claim: The hNs1 loop has strong correlations with β-strands S1-S3.
source: In contrast, the hNs1 loop has strong correlations with β-strands S1-S3 (Figure 7 and Source data 2).

source: These strands, in turn, communicate with H1, switch 1, and the P-loop.

source: We find that h3s5 and h4s6 are largely isolated, suggesting they play a role in forming a stable GPCR-G protein complex but not in the allosteric mechanism that triggers GDP release.

source: This finding is consistent with sequence analysis suggesting these structural elements are important determinants of the specificity of GPCR-Gα interactions (Flock et al., 2017).

claim: S2 and S3 twist relative to S1 and away from H1 during the rate-limiting step.
source: S2 and S3 twist relative to S1 and away from H1 (Figures 2A and 9, Figure 9—figure supplement 1, and Source data 3).

claim: The role for the β-sheets in the activation model is consistent with previous work identifying interactions between S2 and H1.
source: The role for the β-sheets in our model is consistent with previous work identifying interactions between S2 and H1 (Flock et al., 2015), NMR experiments showing chemical exchange in the methyls of S1-S3 upon receptor binding (Toyama et al., 2017), and mutational data.

source: Interestingly, these β-strands and H1 have higher global communication than H5 and the s6h5 loop.

source: This suggests that H1 and the β-sheets integrate conformational information from multiple sources, including the hNs1 loop, and not just H5.

source: The importance of the β sheets and H1 for allosteric communication is consistent with their conservation (Sun et al., 2015), which may not simply reflect the role they play in protein folding and stability, as had been suggested previously (Sun et al., 2015; Hatley et al., 2003).
evidence: This is an inference based on the simulation results, with citations to Sun et al., 2015 and Hatley et al., 2003.

claim: Switch 2 has strong correlations with the nucleotide-binding site, especially switch 1.
source: We also find that switch 2 has strong correlations with the nucleotide-binding site, especially switch 1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Source data 2).

source: Given that switch 2 is a major component of the interface between Gα and Gβ, this communication could enable GDP release to trigger dissociation of Gα from Gβγ.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed correlations and the known role of switch 2.

claim: Switch 2 dynamics are impacted prior to GDP release.
source: These findings are consistent with previous kinetic studies postulating that switch 2 dynamics are impacted prior to GDP release (Herrmann et al., 2004).

source: For example, we identify an important role for coupling from H5 to the s6h5 loop and H1 that is consistent with a previously proposed universal mechanism for G protein activation.

source: Strands S1-S3 and H1 serve as hubs in this network, simultaneously integrating information from both H5 and the hNs1 loop.

source: Our observation is consistent with previous postulates that information flows from H5 and hNs1 to H1 (Preininger et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Preininger et al., 2013.

claim: By focusing analysis on secondary structure elements and residues that are shared across all Gα homologs, the model likely captures a universal 'skeleton' of changes involved in Gα activation.
source: However, by focusing our analysis on secondary structure elements and residues that are shared across all Gα homologs, our model likely captures a universal 'skeleton' of changes involved in Gα activation, expanding upon a previously proposed universal mechanism for Gα activation (Flock et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference about the generalizability of the model, with a citation to Flock et al., 2015.

claim: The consistency of the model with a wide variety of structural and biochemical data suggests that it is a promising foundation for future efforts to understand the determinants of GPCR-Gα interaction specificity, how mutations cause aberrant signaling and disease, and how small molecule inhibitors modulate Gα activation.
source: The consistency of our model with a wide variety of structural and biochemical data suggests that it is a promising foundation for future efforts to understand the determinants of GPCR-Gα interaction specificity, how mutations cause aberrant signaling and disease, and how small molecule inhibitors modulate Gα activation.

claim: The model adds weight to the growing appreciation for the fact that a protein's spontaneous fluctuations encode considerable information about its functional dynamics.
source: Our model also adds weight to the growing appreciation for the fact that a protein's spontaneous fluctuations encode considerable information about its functional dynamics (Koehl et al., 2018; Draper-Joyce et al., 2018; García-Nafría et al., 2018; Kang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about the broader implications of the work, with citations to recent studies (Koehl et al., 2018; Draper-Joyce et al., 2018; García-Nafría et al., 2018; Kang et al., 2018).

claim: The combination of metadynamics and MSMs is expected to prove valuable for understanding other slow conformational changes and unbinding processes.
source: In the future, we expect this methodology will prove valuable for understanding other slow conformational changes and unbinding processes.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential future applications of the methodology.

claim: The crystal structure of Gα from the heterotrimeric Gαq protein (PDB entry 3AH8) was used as the initial structure for simulations.
source: We used the crystal structure of Gα from the heterotrimeric Gαq protein (PDB entry 3AH8) as the initial structure to set up our simulations (Nishimura et al., 2010).
evidence: This describes the starting structure for the simulations, with a citation to Nishimura et al., 2010.

claim: The first 36 residues were removed prior to simulation, as they come from Gαi.
source: The first 36 residues were removed prior to simulation, as they come from Gαi, along with the Gβ and Gγ subunits which were removed to minimize the system size and maximize our chances of observing GDP release (Oldham and Hamm, 2008).
evidence: This describes the system preparation, with a citation to Oldham and Hamm, 2008.

claim: The Gβ and Gγ subunits were removed to minimize the system size and maximize chances of observing GDP release.
source: The first 36 residues were removed prior to simulation, as they come from Gαi, along with the Gβ and Gγ subunits which were removed to minimize the system size and maximize our chances of observing GDP release (Oldham and Hamm, 2008).
evidence: This describes the rationale for system preparation, with a citation to Oldham and Hamm, 2008.

claim: A single Mg2+ ion was added coordinating the phosphate groups of GDP as its presence accelerates GDP release.
source: A single Mg2+ ion was added coordinating the phosphate groups of GDP as its presence accelerates GDP release (Zhang et al., 2000).
evidence: This describes the system preparation, with a citation to Zhang et al., 2000.

claim: The final system consists of one GDP, one Gαq, 57 Cl−1, 64 Na+1, one Mg2+, and 18696 TIP3P water molecules, for a total of 61,893 atoms.
source: The final system consists of one GDP, one Gαq, 57 Cl−1, 64 Na+1, one Mg2+, and 18696 TIP3P water molecules, for a total of 61,893 atoms.
evidence: This describes the composition of the simulated system.

claim: Molecular dynamics simulations were carried out using Gromacs and the AMBER03 force field.
source: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were carried out using Gromacs (Abraham et al., 2015; Van Der Spoel et al., 2005) and the AMBER03 force field (Duan et al., 2003).
evidence: This describes the simulation software and force field used, with citations.

claim: The force field parameters of GDP were obtained from the AMBER Parameter Database.
source: The force field parameters of GDP were obtained from the AMBER Parameter Database (http://research.bmh.manchester.ac.uk/bryce/amber) (Meagher et al., 2003).
evidence: This describes the source of GDP parameters, with a citation to Meagher et al., 2003.

claim: 100 parallel simulations of the GDP bound state were performed on Folding@home for an aggregate simulation time of 35.3 μs.
source: We performed 100 parallel simulations of the GDP bound state on the Folding@home (Shirts and Pande, 2000) distributed computing environment for an aggregate simulation time of 35.3 μs.
evidence: This describes the simulation protocol, with a citation to Shirts and Pande, 2000.

claim: Metadynamics simulations were run on PLUMED.
source: From these states, three representative structures were chosen with inter-domain angles of −6° (Conf. 1),–10° (Conf. 2), and −26.6° (Conf. 3) as starting conformations for metadynamics simulations, which were run on PLUMED (Tribello et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the software used for metadynamics, with a citation to Tribello et al., 2014.

claim: Two collective variables were defined for metadynamics simulations: the distance between GDP's phosphate groups and the backbone of Lys52G.H1.1-Thr54G.H1.3 in Gαq subunit (CV1), and the RMSD of GDP to the starting conformation (CV2).
source: We defined two collective variables for our metadynamics simulations: 1) the distance between GDP's phosphate groups and the backbone of Lys52G.H1.1-Thr54G.H1.3 in Gαq subunit (CV1), and 2) the RMSD of GDP to the starting conformation (CV2).
evidence: This describes the collective variables used in metadynamics.

claim: The string method was applied to detect potential release pathways from metadynamics simulations.
source: We then applied the string method (Maragliano et al., 2006) to detect potential release pathways and use these conformations as the seeds for simulations in step 3.
evidence: This describes the methodology, with a citation to Maragliano et al., 2006.

claim: 2085 conformations were extracted along potential GDP release pathways from metadynamics.
source: We applied this method (Maragliano and Vanden-Eijnden, 2007; Maragliano et al., 2014) to obtain a minimum free energy path, extracting 2085 conformations along potential GDP release pathways.
evidence: This describes the number of conformations extracted, with citations to Maragliano and Vanden-Eijnden, 2007 and Maragliano et al., 2014.

claim: CARDS measures communication between every pair of dihedrals via both correlated changes in structural motions and dynamical behavior.
source: To determine how the GPCR- and GDP-binding regions communicate with one another, we applied the CARDS (Singh and Bowman, 2017) methodology to simulations of the GDP-bound state of Gαq. CARDS measures communication between every pair of dihedrals via both correlated changes in structural motions and dynamical behavior.
evidence: This describes the CARDS methodology, with a citation to Singh and Bowman, 2017.

claim: Protein conformations were clustered into 5040 states using a hybrid k-center/k-medoids method with 1.8 Å cutoff.
source: First, we clustered protein conformations into 5040 states using a hybrid k-center/k-medoids method with 1.8 Å cutoff.
evidence: This describes the clustering methodology used for MSM construction.

claim: The GDP-binding state was clustered into 321 states using the automatic partitioning algorithm (APM) with a residence time of 2 ns.
source: Then we clustered the GDP-binding state into 321 states using the automatic partitioning algorithm (APM) (Sheong et al., 2015) with a residence time of 2 ns.
evidence: This describes the clustering methodology, with a citation to Sheong et al., 2015.

claim: By combining the assignments from protein conformations and the GDP-binding states, a total of 221,965 states were obtained.
source: By combining the assignments from protein conformations and the GDP-binding states, we obtained a total of 221,965 states.
evidence: This describes the total number of states in the MSM.

claim: The implied timescales of the MSM show Markovian behavior with a lag time of 5 ns.
source: The implied timescales of this MSM show Markovian behavior with a lag time of 5 ns (Swope et al., 2004). (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This describes the validation of the MSM, with a citation to Swope et al., 2004 and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: The disorder of every residue was measured by computing Shannon entropy of each dihedral.
source: The disorder of every residue was measured by computing Shannon entropy (Shannon, 1948) of each dihedral as they are natural degrees of freedom for describing protein dynamics.
evidence: This describes the methodology for quantifying disorder, with a citation to Shannon, 1948.

claim: Transition path theory was used to find the highest flux paths from the bound state to the unbound state.
source: We used transition path theory (TPT) (Noé et al., 2009; Weinan and Vanden-Eijnden, 2006) to find the highest flux paths from the bound state to the unbound state (Metzner et al., 2009).
evidence: This describes the methodology, with citations to Noé et al., 2009; Weinan and Vanden-Eijnden, 2006; and Metzner et al., 2009.

claim: The bound state was defined as all clusters that satisfied two criteria: (i) GDP is within 6 Å of the backbone atoms of Lys52-Thr54, and (ii) GDP has an RMSD <0.5 Å to its crystallographic conformation.
source: The bound state was defined as all clusters that satisfied two criteria: (i) GDP is within 6 Å of the backbone atoms of Lys52-Thr54, and (ii) GDP has an RMSD <0.5 Å to its crystallographic conformation.
evidence: This describes the operational definition of the bound state for TPT analysis.

claim: The unbound state was defined as all clusters with GDP > 55 Å from the binding pocket.
source: The unbound state was defined as all clusters with GDP > 55 Å from the binding pocket.
